background.definition: A rib fracture is a structural break in the continuity of a rib, its epiphyseal plate, or cartilaginous joint surface.

list.listitem: In one study, 10% of all patients admitted for trauma had rib fractures.

There is a two-fold higher risk of future fracture of the wrist, hip, or rib, in older individuals who sustain a rib fracture, regardless of bone density findings; on the other hand, a history of previous fracture, low hip bone mineral density, old age, and osteoporosis, lead to a higher risk of sustaining a rib fracture.
Future fractures of the spine, ribs, and wrist are more likely in women of all ages with a history of a previous rib fracture.
Blunt force trauma, the most common mechanism being motor vehicle accident.
Recreational activities (especially young adults).
Falls (especially elderly).
Severe coughing or hard straining (especially in osteoporosis).
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
Child abuse.
Athletes in sports with overhead, forced, recurring movements of the arms (eg, rowing, throwing sports, golfers) developing rib stress fractures usually of the fourth to ninth ribs.
Penetrating injuries to the chest wall.
Post stereotactic radiotherapy for peripheral lung cancer (9/42 in one study).
Blunt trauma to the semirigid chest wall causes a sudden deformity that may lead to a rib fracture.
An increased incidence of rib fractures has been observed in patients with hyperparathyroidism and those with a history of glucocorticoid steroid use.
The risk of a recurrent rib fracture is significantly increased with a history of a previous low-trauma rib fracture.
Order standard PA and lateral CXRs, which can identify most rib fractures. Ultrasound is an acceptable alternative.C
Order a skeletal survey for any child with rib fractures suspected to have been abused, and look for multiple rib fractures in various stages of healing. C
Seventeen percent (17%) of rib fractures due to child abuse are missed on initial x-rays.
Order a bone scan if radiographs are normal and the level of suspicion of rib fracture remains high. C
A CT scan may be ordered to check for internal organ or vessel injury, if suspected. C

Patients typically present with chest pain on inspiration, coughing, or moving. They may also have hemoptysis and/or dyspnea. A history of trauma can often be elicited, and the area of the chest wall that hurts often corresponds to this history.

Rib stress fractures usually present insidiously with activity or as pain in the affected extremity with repetitive loading, usually with no recent history of trauma. Instead, a history of increased training and pain on weight bearing may be elicited. New-onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea due to a hemothorax, symptoms similar to those of pulmonary embolism, may occur in patients with multiple or displaced rib fractures, 18 hours to 6 days after the injury date.

On physical examination, there may be tenderness to palpation, crepitus, ecchymosis, and chest wall deformities. A rib fracture is strongly suggested by severe point tenderness on a specific rib or focal tenderness caused by compression of the ribcage away from the site of the actual pain. Rib fractures that are isolated and nondisplaced may present only as point tenderness.

Flail chest is caused by the fracture of three or more adjacent ribs in two or more places, resulting with a free-floating segment of chest wall that moves paradoxically: inward with inspiration, and outward with expiration, opposite the direction of the surrounding rib cage. Pulmonary contusion is associated with this pattern of injury.

Rib fractures may lead to specific signs of ventilation insufficiency such as cyanosis, tachypnea, retractions, and the use of accessory muscles for ventilation. Anxiety and agitation are more nonspecific signs.

If rib fractures are suspected or diagnosed, rule out a pneumothorax, a hemothorax, a pulmonary contusion, an aortic injury, and/or an abdominal solid organ injury. Diminished breath sounds suggest either a pneumothorax or a pulmonary contusion.

Low rib fractures, right-sided rib fractures, female sex, young age, and a severe thoracic injury all increase the probability of a liver injury. The chance of sustaining a splenic injury is increased by low, left-sided rib fractures, particularly, in the young and severely injured.

Most rib fractures can be identified with standard PA and lateral CXRs. Rib views are not recommended for adults or the elderly; they may be helpful in children. Delayed pneumothorax or hemothorax may be ruled out with follow-up PA and lateral chest x-rays 6 hours after significant trauma to patients who initially appear not to require admission.
If a widened mediastinum is seen on CXR of a patient with a suspected first or second rib fracture, arteriography may be appropriate to rule out vascular injury or other injury to the mediastinum.
A systematic review of 6 studies with 663 patients compared ultrasound with CT for diagnosis of rib fracture. USN was 89.3% sensitive and 98.4% specific, with LR+ 56 and LR- 0.11.

A bone scan is more useful than MRI or CT for diagnosing rib fractures not seen with radiographs; CT does not always demonstrate rib fractures unless 2-mm-thick scan sections are used. CT and MRI are useful in patients with severe trauma to not only look for rib fracture, but also evaluate other structures.

Costochondral separation, subacute rib fractures, and multiple rib fractures or injuries are well-detected by a bone scan, which is especially useful when plain radiographs are not able to demonstrate these.
Adding oblique views of the ribs to a skeletal survey increases the detection of rib fractures in children being evaluated for child abuse.

One systematic review suggests that lung ultrasound may be superior to chest radiography, though limitations of the included studies do not allow for a recommendation to replace chest radiography with lung ultrasound as a first line study.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation and management.
See for a suggested approach to management.
Give NSAIDs (with or without opioids) or an intercostal nerve block to relieve pain due to rib fracture. A
Restrict any pain-inciting activity for 4 to 6 weeks, gradually increase activity as tolerated, and use incentive spirometry to prevent atelectasis. C
Additional pain relief may be achievable by using rib belts or flak jackets without significantly compromising respiratory parameters. B
Pain control, either with NSAIDs (with or without opiates) or with an intercostal nerve block, is the cornerstone of the management of rib fractures.

In a retrospective study of patients with multiple rib fractures receiving ketorolac versus patients who did not, ketorolac was associated with decreased frequency of pneumonia, more ventilator-free days, and more ICU-free days.

Epidural analgesia with bupivacaine and fentanyl has been shown to provide more adequate pain control than patient-controlled analgesia with morphine. In a meta-analysis of 8 small RCTs, there was no benefit of epidural analgesia on mortality or ICU or hospital length of stay compared to other analgesic modalities in adult patients with traumatic rib fractures; the duration of mechanical ventilation was decreased with use of thoracic epidural analgesia but was associated with hypotension.

There are mixed results based off several studies over the effectiveness of Lidocaine patches: one showing no significant difference in pain control, but another showing decreased length of hospitalstay and use of other pain medications.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of the oral probiotic Lactobacillus casei Shirota in patients with a single rib fracture revealed more effective pain relief in those using the probiotic.
Persistent pain is the rationale for a surgical referral and is often due to non-union, which is rare and may not require surgery.

A prospective cohort study identified 100 patients with surgical stabilization of rib fracture (SSRF), and was able to contact 50 for follow-up by telephone. Patients were pain-free an average of 5.4 weeks after discharge, and back to work at 8.5 weeks.

A randomized trial of 207 patients with displaced rib fractures with a flail chest or non-flail chest injuries with severe chest wall deformity compared surgical with nnono-surgical management. Patients with operative treatment had less need for mechanical ventilation and lower mortality (6% vs 0%, p = 0.01).

For patients with flail chest injury, a systematic review found 3 studies with a total of 123 patients that compared surgical with non-surgical treatment. Patients undergoing surgical fixation, there was a lower likelihood of pneumonia (RR 0.5, 95% CI 0.3-0.7), shorter duration of mechanical ventilation (6.5 days) and ICU stay (5.2 days), and less need for tracheostomy (RR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2-0.7). There was a trend toward lower mortality but it was not significant (RR 0.6, 95% CI 0.1-2.4).

A meta-analysis concluded that hospitalized patients receiving surgical management for rib fractures, compared to non-surgical approaches, experienced reduced time of hospitalization, intensive care and mechanical ventilation, as well as lowered rates of mortality, pulmonary infection, and tracheotomy.
A randomized trial found no benefit of surgery in patients with severe chest injury and rib fractures but without flail chest.
Incentive spirometry may be useful in preventing atelectasis in patients with rib fractures.
Restriction from pain-inciting activity for 4 to 6 weeks, with gradual return to normal activities, is part of the management.

There is inconsistent evidence regarding rib belts. Some studies show that additional pain relief can be achieved by using rib belts or flak jackets without significantly compromising respiratory parameters. Other studies show that use of rib belts or flak jackets increases the incidence of complications.

An unblinded, randomized controlled trial evaluating serratus anterior plane block to reduce acute rib fracture pain revealed that those receiving the block used less tramodol than those in the standard/usual therapy group, suggesting that serratus anterior plan blocks may be a useful tool in acute rib fracture pain control.
See algorithm in .
Most patients with three or more rib fractures should be hospitalized.
Elderly patients with six or more rib fractures may need ICU care.
Conservative management generally leads to a good prognosis in virtually all rib fractures, with healing and return to function in about 6 weeks.
However, one study found that among 203 patients with rib fractures, 59% to 76% had pain lasting more than 2 months after injury.

Among a national database of 35,467 patients with traumatic rib fractures, the number of rib fractures did not predict patient outcome (including comorbidity, complications, intensive care unit duration, ventilator duration, length of stay, and death). However, age and overall trauma did predict poorer outcomes.
In one cohort study, injury severity score and presence of a parenchymal injury on plain CXR were independent predictors of subsequent respiratory failure.
A chest trauma scoring system found that bilateral rib fracture and the number of rib fractures were important predictors of morbidity and mortality in patients with chest wall trauma.

A mortality risk score model was studied that used five risk factors: age (2 points for every decade over 20), Glasgow Coma Score <15 (2 points), ventilation required (3 points), caused by cardiopulmonary resuscitation (3 points), and number of comorbidities (1 point each). It was determined that less than 6 points is consistent with 1% observed mortality, 6 to 10 points predicts 5% mortality, 11 to 15 points predicts 22% mortality, and 16 or more points predicts 46% mortality.
A retrospective study of patients admitted to a Level 1 Trauma center revealed that patients with an FVC <1 had significantly higher rates of complications compared to those with an FVC >1.
Use of percentage predicted FVC to triage patients with rib fractures may have value in deciding whether or not to transfer to an ICU, and potentially reduce ICU and hospital lengths of stay.
Rib series, which use bone exposure and include oblique views of the chest wall, should be considered for elderly patients who present with multiple rib fractures with increased morbidity rates.
Elderly patients with six or more rib fractures may require ICU care.
To prevent future fractures, older men and women who sustain rib fractures should be evaluated for probable osteoporosis, and treatment started as appropriate.
Strategies to prevent falling should be considered to decrease the risk of sustaining rib fractures in both sexes.
The risk for rib fractures increases with an increased risk of falling, heavy alcohol use, and low bone mineral density in older women.

To prevent the increased risk of fractures (including rib fractures) in postmenopausal women, medications such as alendronate, risedronate, and etidronate may be considered, especially if independent clinical risk factors, age, and T-score indicate these may be helpful. For the same group of women who cannot tolerate the above, denosumab may be a good option.

A child with rib fractures suspected to have been abused should undergo a skeletal survey, which may reveal multiple rib fractures in various stages of healing. In a retrospective review of prospectively collected data from one trauma center, the odds of rib (14.4 times), tibia/fibula (6.3 times), radius/ulna (5.8 times), and clavicle fractures (4.4 times) were significantly higher in child abuse victims versus accidental trauma patients.
In a systematic review of 10 studies with 1396 children with rib fracture, abuse prevalence was 67% to 82% for infants under age 12 months, compared with 29% in older infants (age 12-35 months).

In a retrospective chart review of sequential chest radiographs in children 0 to 2 years-old, 0.05% of chest radiographs revealed incidental rib fractures. Three of these 5 chest xrays were suggestive of nonaccidental trauma, suggesting unreported and incidental rib fractures in children may represent evidence of abuse.
In another retrospective study, 17% of rib fractures were missed on initial skeletal survery, half of which were found with low-dose CT scan at subsequent visits.

Severe physical abuse is a valid consideration for any rib fracture in infancy, and will require action on the part of the physician (reporting to the appropriate authorities) to ensure safe child protection outcomes.

Systematic review related to rib fractures in children from 1980 to 2020 revealed that in children under 3 years old presenting with non-motor vehicle crash related rib fractures, 77% were abused. (Mitchell et al. Acad Emerg Med 2021)

algorithm.title: Algorithm for Screening and Diagnosis of Patient with Suspected Rib Fracture.

cell.label: Unstable patient and/or possible complication (pneumothorax or hemothorax), ≥3 fractured ribs, liver or spleen laceration, cardiac or pulmonary contusion, mediastinal or aortic injury, superior or displaced rib fractures, possible child abuse?
Perform appropriate emergency procedure (if needed), stabilize, arrange to send to emergency room, monitor while awaiting transfer.
Obtain history and physical examination to substantiate and characterize suspected rib fracture(s), order PA and lateral CXRs. Emergent condition (eg, pneumothorax, hemothorax)?
Control pain (NSAIDs with or without opioids, nerve blocks), restrict inciting activity, use incentive spirometer as tolerated to prevent atelectasis.
Follow-up in 4 to 6 weeks: Is patient pain-free with normal activities?
Rehab to allow return to sports (possibly with rib belt or flak jacket) and work, as tolerated.
Follow-up in 6 to 8 weeks: Is patient pain free with normal activities?
Obtain dedicated rib series (bone exposure and oblique views of chest wall).
Rule out rib fracture(s) as unlikely, consider other differentials.
